extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of public administration, municipal reformers, civic leaders, and legislators
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for judging and designing city government structures and reforms (charters, electoral systems, fiscal limits, administrative organization, and accountability mechanisms). Extracts practical remedies and pitfalls for improving municipal administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and consistency of municipal statutes
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutes referring to public improvements have been modified, superseded, and repealed so often that it is difficult to ascertain which statutes are in force; this uncertainty leads to incessant litigation and expense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chief-Justice Church quote: the multiplication and conflict of legislation produce litigation and burdens both public and private; remedying this requires legislative simplification and statutory stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation of local popular control and responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Local popular control — with accountability to local citizens — is a foundational principle; transferring control of municipal resources to the State capitol departs from this principle and amplifies corruption by extending the reach of lobbying and patronage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transfer of control to state level caused lobby traffic and spread of municipal corruption beyond territorial limits; reforms should aim to restore local responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevention of special legislation and state interference
rubrics_metrics.description: Limit the legislature's power to pass special acts relating to cities and separate state and city elections to reduce meddling and instability in municipal affairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The New York commission's recommendations and later charter changes (e.g., separating elections, restricting borrowing, extending mayoral appointment/removal powers) are cited as improvements though not perfect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merit-based civil service (civil service reform)
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish examinations as tests for admission to city posts and provide fixed terms or tenure during good behavior to prevent partisan displacement of civil servants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Item (a): civil service reform reduces vulnerability of employees to partisan chiefs who displace them for party adherents or friends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive stability through longer terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Lengthen terms of service for the mayor and heads of departments to give them a more assured position and reduce the frequency of disruptive elections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Item (b): many recent charters have lengthened terms to some extent to promote stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentrated executive power (strong-mayor model)
rubrics_metrics.description: Vest broad executive power in the mayor while restricting the city legislature to legislative duties and voting supplies, thereby concentrating responsibility for administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Item (c): described as a 'cure or kill' remedy—effective if voters elect able honest men, but risky when voters are apathetic; historical experience mixed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear assignment of responsibility and accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Create methods to fix public responsibility on specific governing persons and bodies; diffuse responsibility (mayor blaming council, bicameral chambers blaming each other, multiple boards) prevents effective reproof or commendation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text gives examples of mayors and legislatures excusing failures by pointing to other bodies; multiplicity of elective posts dilutes voters' ability to hold individuals accountable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit the multiplication of elective posts
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid greatly increasing the number of important elective officers, since multiplying elective posts lessens the effectiveness of popular control and disperses the impact of the ballot-box.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seth Low: choosing among a multitude of unimportant officers involves loss of popular power; too many elective offices subsides the 'blow' of the popular will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Election of council members at large (general ticket)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer election of a city legislature or one branch on a general ticket instead of by wards to broaden representatives' view beyond local ward interests and reduce parochial bargaining over contracts and improvements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Item (d): ward-elected aldermen tend to prioritize ward gains and barter with other wards; general ticket encourages city-wide responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fiscal constraints tied to assessed value (taxing and borrowing limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Limit taxing and borrowing powers by reference to the assessed value of taxable property (constitutional/legislative debt limits) to restrain municipal indebtedness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Item (e): while often effective in diminishing abuses, such restrictions can be evaded (e.g., by raising assessments or parallel borrowing by overlapping bodies), and may force piecemeal execution of improvements that would be cheaper done at once.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct democracy mechanisms: Initiative, Referendum, Recall
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce initiative (citizen-submitted ordinances), referendum (citizen voting on ordinances passed by council upon petition), and recall (citizen-driven removal elections) to allow citizens to enact, veto, or remove officials and counteract jobbing and corruption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Item (f): these are drastic remedies (example: Los Angeles recall in 1909); they aim to prevent jobbing and improve conduct, but their operation must be observed for long-term effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commission form (Galveston/Des Moines Plan)
rubrics_metrics.description: Replace the mayor-and-council frame with a small board of commissioners elected at large to concentrate responsibility, reduce machine power, and combine executive and legislative functions in few hands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Item (g): plan spreads quickly (as of 1910); expected to work with open primaries, general-ticket elections, recall, and referendum, but not yet mature enough to reveal all defects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Considered public vs. private provision of utilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Carefully evaluate whether water, gas, electricity, and street railways should be municipally owned or left to private corporations, balancing risks of corrupt public management against abuses by private monopolies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author declines long discussion but notes each plan has dangers: private companies can bribe voters and officials; municipal control may rouse citizen interest but can also add patronage opportunities; data: in ~1910, 59 cities left water to private corporations, 101 municipal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordination and intercommunication among boards and officials
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure adequate intercommunication and cooperation among various boards and officials; directly elected boards may feel independent of mayor and council, undermining unified administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text notes lack of intercommunication historically and gives a Philadelphia example where multiple independent authorities could tear up streets with no one responsible for repair.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid office reorganization that merely redistributes patronage
rubrics_metrics.description: Resist creating, abolishing, or reshaping offices solely to transfer emoluments or patronage (e.g., abolishing one office and creating another with same duties to shift rewards).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text describes laws made to change functions or terms of offices to redistribute patronage or retain particular officers—these are reforms to be guarded against when designing charters.
